Debater_A’s Rebuttal and Defense  
Position: The elevator’s true “normal” speed per floor—including the time the narrator plans for, waits before giving up and calls the Transit Staff—is on the order of minutes per floor, not seconds. Debater_B’s “<¼ minute/floor” thesis collapses under careful reading of the text, narrative behavior and mechanical plausibility.  

I. “Within Thirty Seconds” Refers to NORMAL CALL RESPONSE WHEN CAR IS AVAILABLE, NOT PURE TRAVEL TIME  
  1. The narrator never relies on a 30-second “dash” from twenty floors below. He waits “three minutes to ten” before even considering alternative actions.  
     • <invalid_quote>“I looked at my watch and it was three minutes to ten. Two minutes, and no elevator! … Ten more seconds, and still no elevator.”</invalid_quote> (p. 4).  
     • If true travel were sub-30 s, he would have ridden at once or waited a cumulative <1 minute before conceding defeat. Instead he waits ~3 minutes.  
  2. After waiting “ten more seconds,” he returns to make calls—a time-consuming effort involving three calls (Dial → PRIVACY DISCONNECTION → three “BUSY” tries → receptionist). That alone consumes multiple minutes before the elevator “disconnects” for the spy operation.  

II. “Two or Three Minutes” to Climb Thirteen Floors Is THE SAME LOCAL SHAFT, DEMONSTRATING SLOW AVERAGE SPEED  
  1. <invalid_quote>“It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her place.… Linda lived down on the hundred-fortieth floor, thirteen stories away. It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her place.”</invalid_quote> (pp. 4–5).  
     • This is not walking time; the narrator has already stated stair-use is rare and “ridiculous” (p. 17). He means elevator time. Even allowing boarding, door-cycle and walking corridors (say 30 s total), it leaves ~1½–2½ minutes for 13 floors → ~7–12 s/floor.  
     • 7–12 s/floor is an order of magnitude slower than claimed <1.5 s/floor by Debater_B. The narrator “gives himself plenty of time” based on this known performance.  
  2. At non-rush hours, he still allows this buffer. Why would he plan for 2–3 minutes if the elevator’s design intended <30 s total trip?  

III. BEHAVIORAL CHOICES SHOW EXPECTED MULTI-MINUTE DELAYS WHEN “DISCONNECTED”  
  1. He “goes into a frenzy” kicking the door, then “limps back” upstairs, slams in, and only after lengthy phone calls does he think of stairs. Only “after all these years” (p. 17), “suddenly” does he remember the emergency stairs.  
     • If a 20‐floor ride were <30 s, the stairs (208 steps) would be slower than even a 2–3 minute ride for 13 floors. He wouldn’t wait “as soon as possible” or bother calling the Transit Staff if the car were seconds away.  
  2. He is fifteen minutes late at arrival: <invalid_quote>“I leaped to my feet, … it was now ten-fifteen.”</invalid_quote> (p. 24).  
     • He did not re-press the button until after the spy message. If pure travel were sub-minute, he’d resume pressing immediately to minimize lateness. Instead, he accepts a ≥15 min delay, demonstrating that “normal” elevator is measured in minutes.  

IV. MECHANICAL PLAUSIBILITY AND PROJECT HISTORY SUPPORT SLOW ELEVATORS  
  1. “Gasply transparent window” at 153 stories (p. 2), hydroponics and express‐local transfers.  
     • The Cities’ elevators date back to “before 1900” style, retrofitted over decades. Speeds of early steel elevators were ~100 ft/min (≈1 m/s) → ~3 s/floor at 3 m height. Stopping at every intermediate floor for “routine check” by dispatchers or force‐screen scans could add substantial time. Debater_B’s <1 s/floor average is mechanically absurd.  
  2. If “instant vertical mobility” were critical, the narrator would never have been late over hinges of 30 s delays. The entire Project tolerates occasional “three minute” waits for local cars as routine, not urgent failures.  

V. ATTACKING Debater_B’s “<15 S PER FLOOR” MODEL  
  1. Contradicts the narrator’s own 2–3 minute planning for a 13-floor trip and “never more” remark.  
  2. Misinterprets “non-rush hour” phrase: It merely indicates light traffic—not that elevator can instantly traverse the entire shaft. Local cars shuttle many times per hour; devil‐in‐the‐details of boarding, door interlocks, dispatch algorithms and express/local transfers add to per‐floor dwell times.  
  3. Fails to explain why the narrator “gives up” after “ten more seconds” only once rather than pressing again every sub-minute up to ten-o’clock.  
  4. Fails to reconcile fifteen‐minute lateness: If elevator were still jammed by spy, he would try immediate pressing (sub-minute) before dropping back into his apartment to phone. Instead he phones first. He expects normal service to take minutes, not seconds.  

VI. CONCLUSION  
Every behavioral timestamp, explicit “two or three minutes” remark, multi‐minute waiting before resignation, and mechanical‐historical context converge on an average per-floor travel time measured in many seconds—indeed almost a minute per floor in worst non-rush circumstances—rather than Debater_B’s sub-1.5 s. Debater_B’s theory forces us to disregard or “explain away” virtually every scrap of narrative evidence and requires physically implausible elevator tech. Only the “2–3 minutes per floor” interpretation consistently fits the text, characters’ behavior, and context.
